catalog_quote: As a general rule we can say that stress falls on the final syllable. In no case does it occur before the penultimate syllable. Penultimate stress occurs in a lot of proper names and in many derived words with suffixes. If such suffixes are added to a stem with penultimate stress they bear the stress anyway. Apart from the primary stress there is also secondary stress in words which have more than two syllables before the stressed syllable. The secondary stress is alternating. (Geurtjens 1926:3-4) ... [Usher, Newguineaworld 'Marind', paraphrasing Drabbe:] Stress falls on the final syllable of the root, as it does in the distantly-related Lowland Ok family to the northeast; Drabbe (1955: 16) characterizes this as a rise in pitch or tone. ... audit.reasoning: The classification (morphological: root-final stress inside a two-syllable right-edge window, penult stress in suffix-derived forms/names, not computable from syllable count) is correct and is now triple-sourced: (1) the StressTyp2 translation of Geurtjens 1926:3-4 is verbatim in the held st2_dump and I verified it against the Dutch original downloaded from Delpher (pp.3-5), which confirms every clause including the alternating pre-tonic secondary stress and clarifies that a suffix takes the stress only when the base is penult-stressed; (2) Usher's Drabbe paraphrase is verbatim in the held Newguineaworld page; (3) Olsson 2017, the modern 594-pp grammar and best available description, is already held by the project (downloaded by the morphstress reader a day after the catalog reading) and states stress is root-final, realized as higher pitch, weight-insensitive, penult only in derived forms, with prefixal complex a

sources.citation: Olsson, Bruno (2017). The Coastal Marind language. PhD thesis, Nanyang Technological University. 594 pp. hdl 10356/73235. (Already held since 13 Sep at, but NOT used by the 12 Sep catalog reading; read now for this reading.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.25: 'There is no lexical tone. Stress is generally root-final and primarily realized by pitch.' p.60: 'Stress in Marind is characterized by higher pitch on the stressed syllable, so it could alternatively be labeled (pitch) accent... The predominant stress pattern is for the last syllable of a monomorphemic word to be stressed... kana [kaˈna] 'egg', patul [paˈtul] 'boy'. A less frequent pattern in (synchronically) monomorphemic words is for the penultimate syllable to bear stress, as in /ˈa.lo/ 'worm' and /ˈuk.na/ 'fear'. A likely explanation is that these words are historically derived form
